groups.text: A coroutine runs on some thread, but suspend doesn't say which.
The dispatcher in its context picks it, each time the coroutine starts or resumes.
This is Kotlin only: Java has no coroutines.
When you name no dispatcher, launch and async use Dispatchers.Default.
It has one thread per core, and at least two.
On a four-core pod that's four threads, for C P U work.
Run a two hundred millisecond JDBC query there, and the thread sleeps for two hundred milliseconds, doing nothing.
Four requests doing that take every thread, and all C P U work waits.
In the lesson's lab, thirty-two such calls take about one thousand six hundred milliseconds, eight rounds of four, and a tiny C P U task waits about one thousand five hundred milliseconds to start.
Blocking calls belong on Dispatchers.I O, which runs up to sixty-four at once.

There, the thirty-two calls take about two hundred twenty milliseconds, and the tiny task starts within a few milliseconds.
I O and Default share one pool of worker threads.
The split gives them separate budgets: blocking work can fill I O, and Default still has a thread for every core.
To move one piece of work, use withContext.
Loading the rows is a blocking JDBC call.
Rendering the PDF is C P U work.
withContext suspends the caller and runs the block on I O.
Often the same worker keeps going, now counted against I O's limit, and Default's place goes to another thread.

When the block is done, the caller resumes on its own dispatcher, Default, with the rows.
Rendering is C P U work, so it runs there too.
So never block on Default: wrap each blocking call in withContext(Dispatchers.I O), inside the function that blocks.
Calls that already suspend, like delay, need no switch.
When one resource needs its own budget, limitedParallelism makes a view of I O with its own limit, like twenty for a card issuer with twenty connections.
A view owns no threads, and it adds to I O's sixty-four instead of taking a share.
